title: Quantifying Multi-Decadal Terrestrialization in the Upper Mississippi River System with a Composite Hydrology–Vegetation Index
content: Terrestrialization, the conversion of open-water and aquatic-vegetation habitat to terrestrial cover, can reduce backwater and marsh habitat for fish and waterbirds in regulated river–floodplain systems. In the Upper Mississippi River System (UMRS), land-cover change and floodplain inundation are well documented but rarely summarized together in an updatable form. We combined three systemic land-cover surveys (1989, 2000, and 2010/2011), restricted to a common classified extent, with gauge-based annual high-flow days (HFD, 1985–2024) into a two-indicator Floodplain Transition Index (FTI) for four Long Term Resource Monitoring reaches (Pools 4, 8, 13, and 26). Terrestrial fraction differed widely among reaches (0.29–0.77) but decreased by less than 0.04 in each between 1989 and 2010/2011. On the natural floodplain, gross aquatic–terrestrial conversion (5,209 ha) was 4.7 times the net change, which favored aquatic cover. HFD trends were positive but small and non-significant (+0.10 to +0.96 days yr⁻¹). FTI ordered reaches mainly by land cover but changed between epochs mainly with antecedent HFD (91% of within-reach variance). Neither directional hypothesis nor the exploratory depth hypothesis was supported. Reported with its components, FTI can serve as a screening and communication tool that is updated with each survey and shows whether change is hydrologic or land-cover driven.
